Introduction

The objective of Project 2 is to work through importing, tidying and prepping messy data for downstream analysis using tidyr and dplyr. The following datasets have been chosen, stored as raw CSV files, and could be found in my Week 5 Assignment directory on GitHub:

  • Motherboard / Vice’s Car Thefts across the USA (Discussion source)

  • Medical records (Discussion source)

  • Highest Grossing Concert Tours by Women (Discussion source)

Approach

As per the project requirements, each of the datasets will follow the same steps separately:

  1. Import the raw CSV files from the GitHub directory to preserve the original or scrapped structure. If possible, I will mark any blank records as NA, where needed.

  2. Read the csv file and inspect the structure of the files, then try to get the headers / columns to store as variables.

  3. Reshape the datasets from a wide format into a long format using pivot_longer() , which will collapse the columns into rows. We can also drop any blank records here as well in this step, if missed with values_drop_na = TRUE.

  4. Cleaning and tidying the datasets will happen next, to standardize variable names (casing, naming patterns, turning Y -> Yes), convert column/row data types to the appropriate formats (ex. dates, numeric). I’ll double check once more for any missing or NA records to make sure that’s documented and accounted for prior to calculations.

  5. After, I can validate that the cleaned data is matching the unstructured data by verifying missing, duplicates or mislabeled variables are converted to the correct labeling.

  6. Lastly, I’ll explore the cleaned and validated data by creating some graphs and charts with ggplot2 for some simple analysis. Some questions I will have are how do Kia/Hyundai’s share of total vehicle thefts change over time, any correlations between age and BMI with existing conditions, and adjusted vs actual gross for the tour.

Code 
# helper and import chunk
library(tidyverse)
pct_label <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", paste0(round(x * 100), "%"))

First Dataset — Kia/Hyundai thefts

Challenges

  • For the car thefts, I anticipate the blank records being a challenge. The missing theft records from certain locations should not be counted as zeroes, but NA, which I can fix upon import of the file to avoid any complications - na.strings = c("", "NA").

  • Additionally, there are some inconsistencies of formatting of the locations, such as misspellings and the city/county pattern is not always enforced. Those will have to be fixed with a case_when() to catch before analysis.

car_theft_header_rows <- read_csv(car_thefts_raw_url, col_names = FALSE, n_max = 2,
                        col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

car_theft_data_body <- read_csv(car_thefts_raw_url, col_names = FALSE, skip = 2,
                       na = c("", "NA"),
                       col_types = cols(.default = "c")) # skips double header rows

We learn here that the data’s structure is 45 data rows by 211 columns. Column 1 has the month and year from Dec/19 through Aug/23.Row 1 is a merged city header (a name followed by two empty cells) and row 2 repeats Kia/Hyundais, All, Percent for each of 70 geographies. City and measure are values stored as column names, so 9,450 observations sit in 210 columns.

Transformation

Code 
# Each city name appears once per three-column block, so two of every
# three header cells are empty and must be filled downward.
city_row    <- as.character(car_theft_header_rows[1, ])
measure_row <- as.character(car_theft_header_rows[2, ])

header_map <- tibble(
  position = seq_along(city_row),
  city     = str_trim(city_row),
  measure  = str_trim(measure_row)
) |>
  fill(city, .direction = "down")

n_distinct(header_map$city, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 70
Code 
count(header_map, measure) # Output is 70 cities / columns
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  measure          n
  <chr>        <int>
1 All             70
2 Kia/Hyundais    70
3 Percent         70
4 <NA>             1

Trailing space is seen on several cities, which is why str_trim() is needed. Otherwise, later in the transformation process, two separate columns would be created instead of one.

Code 
# Combine city and measure into one name per column. "__" is used as the
# separator because no city name contains it, unlike "_", "," or " ".
new_names <- header_map |>
  mutate(col_name = if_else(position == 1,
                            "month",
                            str_c(city, measure, sep = "__"))) |>
  pull(col_name)

theft_named <- car_theft_data_body |> set_names(new_names)

names(theft_named)[1:7]
[1] "month"                 "Denver__Kia/Hyundais"  "Denver__All"          
[4] "Denver__Percent"       "El Paso__Kia/Hyundais" "El Paso__All"         
[7] "El Paso__Percent"
Code 
theft_long <- theft_named |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -month,
    names_to  = c("city", "measure"),
    names_sep = "__",
    values_to = "value"
  )

dim(theft_long)   # expect 9450 x 4
[1] 9450    4
Code 
theft_tidy <- theft_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  rename(
    kia_hyundai_thefts = `Kia/Hyundais`,
    all_thefts         = All,
    pct_reported       = Percent
  )

dim(theft_tidy)   # expect 3150 x 5
[1] 3150    5

Variable types and naming

Code 
theft_tidy <- theft_tidy |>
  mutate(
    # Turning source data format from "Dec/19" -> 2019-12-01
    month = parse_date(as.character(month), format = "%b/%y"),

    # Strip comma separators from numeric column: "1,014" -> 1014
    across(c(kia_hyundai_thefts, all_thefts), parse_number),

    # "8%" -> 8 -> 0.08, stored as a proportion for consistency
    pct_reported = parse_number(pct_reported) / 100,

    # Manually correcting typos and inconsistent formatting
    city = case_when(
      city == "Cincinatti"        ~ "Cincinnati",
      city == "Corpus Cristi, TX" ~ "Corpus Christi, TX",
      city == "Irving, Texas"     ~ "Irving, TX",
      TRUE ~ city
    )
  ) |>
  # Recompute the share rather than trusting the source column, which is
  # rounded to whole percents and blank for several reporting cities.
  mutate(
    pct_kia_hyundai = if_else(all_thefts > 0,
                              kia_hyundai_thefts / all_thefts,
                              NA_real_)
  )

theft_tidy |>
  summarise(
    `City-months`      = n(),

    `Kia count only`   = sum(!is.na(kia_hyundai_thefts) &  is.na(all_thefts)),
    `Total count only` = sum( is.na(kia_hyundai_thefts) & !is.na(all_thefts)),

  )
# A tibble: 1 × 5
  `City-months` `Both counts` `Kia count only` `Total count only`
          <int>         <int>            <int>              <int>
1          3150          2793              143                145
# ℹ 1 more variable: `Neither count` <int>

Blank cells are kept as NA and not marked as zero. Some cities, such as Virginia Beach, Norfolk and Miami never report a total theft count; Frisco and Lincoln never report a Kia/Hyundai count; Atlanta, San Antonio and Henderson begin reporting only in January 2021. Treating those blanks as zeros would create problems with our data and analysis, so we will drop any incomplete records from theft_tidy here.

Analysis

The analysis compares each city’s mean monthly Kia/Hyundai share of all reported vehicle thefts between two periods, split at July 2022 — the month the theft technique got popular on social media. The summary statistic is the difference in those means, expressed in percentage points.

Code 
share_change <- theft_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(pct_kia_hyundai)) |>
  mutate(period = if_else(month < as.Date("2022-07-01"), "pre", "post")) |>
  group_by(city, period) |>
  summarise(months = n(), mean_share = mean(pct_kia_hyundai), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = c(months, mean_share)) |>
  filter(months_pre >= 12, months_post >= 6) |>
  mutate(change_pp = (mean_share_post - mean_share_pre) * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(change_pp))

nrow(share_change)   # cities meeting the coverage threshold
[1] 63
Code 
share_change |>
  slice_max(change_pp, n = 10) |>
  transmute(
    City                       = city,
    `Share before (%)`         = round(mean_share_pre  * 100, 1),
    `Share Jul 2022 on (%)`    = round(mean_share_post * 100, 1),
    `Change (pct. points)`     = round(change_pp, 1),
    `Months (pre / post)`      = str_c(months_pre, " / ", months_post)
  )
Code 
top_cities <- share_change |> slice_max(change_pp, n = 6) |> pull(city)

theft_tidy |>
  filter(city %in% top_cities, !is.na(pct_kia_hyundai)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = pct_kia_hyundai, color = city)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2022-07-01"),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_label) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(
    x       = "Month",
    y       = "Share of all reported vehicle thefts",
    color   = "City",
    caption = "Source: Motherboard / VICE News police-record dataset, Dec 2019 - Aug 2023"
  )

Conclusions

The tidy dataset holds 3150 city-months, of which 2792 have both counts reported, leaving 63 cities with enough coverage to compare periods. The largest increase is in Rochester, NY, where the Kia/Hyundai share of reported vehicle thefts rose from 9.8% before July 2022 to 52.9% afterward — a gain of 43.1 percentage points. The median change across all 63 qualifying cities is 13.5 percentage points.

Figure 1 shows the shift is abrupt rather than gradual, with most of the rise concentrated in the second half of 2022 and sustained through August 2023. That pattern is consistent with a known vehicle vulnerability becoming widely exploited at a point in time, rather than a slow change in the composition of the vehicle fleet, which would produce a gentle trend across the whole series.

Two limitations follow from the missing-value decisions above. The comparison covers reporting agencies only: 358 city-months lack at least one count and are excluded throughout. And three of the 70 geographies are counties rather than cities — Riverside County CA, Montgomery County MD and Prince George’s County MD — so the units are reporting jurisdictions, not a uniform set of municipalities.

Second Dataset — Medical records

Challenges

  • Like the first dataset, I also anticipate the blank records being a challenge here with the medical records. The missing records from certain locations should not be counted as zeroes, but NA, which I can fix upon import of the file to avoid any complications - na.strings = c("", "NA").

  • Certain variables, such as Smoker, has inconsistent labeling and will need to be reformatted to one standardized pattern.

Third Dataset — Highest Grossing Concert Tours by Women

Dataset B — Patient clinical records

Data source

Synthetic patient records distributed as course teaching data: 100 patients with demographic, clinical and administrative fields, admitted during calendar 2023. Committed unmodified to data/raw/medical_records_raw.csv and read here from its GitHub raw URL. The data is simulated, so results below describe the dataset itself and carry no clinical meaning.

Code 
medical_records_raw_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shanicesmith98/data-607-assignments/refs/heads/main/week-5-assignment/realworld_medical_dirty_dataset.csv"

# This file encodes missingness three different ways: empty cells, the
# literal text "nan", and the literal text "N/A". All three are declared
# here so they arrive as NA rather than as data.
medical_records_raw_data <- read_csv(
  medical_records_raw_url,
  na = c("", "nan", "N/A"),
  col_types = cols(
    Patient_ID     = col_character(),
    Age            = col_double(),
    Gender         = col_character(),
    Blood_Pressure = col_double(),
    Cholesterol    = col_double(),
    BMI            = col_double(),
    Smoker         = col_character(),
    Diagnosis      = col_character(),
    Admission_Date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    Notes          = col_character()
  )
)

Declaring na at read time is the single most consequential decision for this file. Omit it and "nan" becomes a legitimate category: Gender gains a sixth level with 15 members and Smoker a fifth with 20, both of which would then appear in every grouped summary as though they were real values.

The raw file is 100 rows by 10 columns, one row per patient, with IDs P1000 through P1099 and no duplicates. It is already close to tidy in the sense that each row is one observational unit — but four of the columns (Age, Blood_Pressure, Cholesterol, BMI) are four separate measurements of the same patient, which forces any cross-measurement comparison into repetitive, column-by-column code. Column names are also inconsistently cased and the categorical columns carry several spellings of the same value.

Gender holds five spellings of two values (Male, MALE, male, Female, FEMALE). Smoker mixes Yes/Y and No/N. Admission_Date is the one column needing no treatment: valid ISO-8601 throughout.

Transformation steps

Consistent variable names

Code 
# snake_case throughout, with units folded into the name where helpful.
med <- medical_records_raw_data |>
  rename(
    patient_id     = Patient_ID,
    age_years      = Age,
    gender         = Gender,
    blood_pressure = Blood_Pressure,
    cholesterol    = Cholesterol,
    bmi            = BMI,
    smoker_raw     = Smoker,
    diagnosis      = Diagnosis,
    admission_date = Admission_Date,
    notes          = Notes
  )

blood_pressure keeps a neutral name on purpose. The file records a single number per patient in the 120–160 range, which is almost certainly systolic pressure, but the source provides no legend — so the column is not renamed systolic_bp, and the assumption is stated here rather than built into the data.

Standardising inconsistent values

Code 
med <- med |>
  mutate(
    # Five spellings collapse to two with one title-case call.
    gender = str_to_title(gender),

    # Yes/Y and No/N become a logical, which makes later proportions trivial.
    is_smoker = case_when(
      smoker_raw %in% c("Yes", "Y") ~ TRUE,
      smoker_raw %in% c("No",  "N") ~ FALSE,
      TRUE ~ NA
    ),

    # Diagnosis has BOTH a "None" level and missing values; these mean
    # different things and are kept distinct. "None" = examined, nothing
    # found. NA = not recorded. An explicit label makes the difference
    # visible in every grouped table below.
    diagnosis_group = if_else(is.na(diagnosis), "Not recorded", diagnosis)
  ) |>
  select(-smoker_raw)   # drop the raw column now that is_smoker exists

2 Male      53

Reshaping the measurements to long form

Code 
med_tidy <- med |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(age_years, blood_pressure, cholesterol, bmi),
    names_to  = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Units travel with the data instead of being hard-coded into headers.
    unit = case_when(
      measure == "age_years"      ~ "years",
      measure == "blood_pressure" ~ "mmHg",
      measure == "cholesterol"    ~ "mg/dL",
      measure == "bmi"            ~ "kg/m2"
    ),
    measure_label = case_when(
      measure == "age_years"      ~ "Age",
      measure == "blood_pressure" ~ "Blood pressure",
      measure == "cholesterol"    ~ "Cholesterol",
      measure == "bmi"            ~ "BMI"
    ),
    # One combined label so figure facets carry their units
    facet_label = str_c(measure_label, " (", unit, ")")
  )

dim(med_tidy)   # expect 400 x 10
[1] 400  12

The id columns — patient_id, gender, is_smoker, diagnosis, admission_date, notes — are left untouched by the pivot because they describe the patient, not the measurement. Only the four measured quantities move. The result is 100 patients × 4 measurements = 400 rows, which is the grain that lets one group_by() answer a question about all four measurements at once.

Missing-value decisions

Code 
med_tidy |>
  group_by(Measurement = facet_label) |>
  summarise(
    Patients   = n(),
    Reported   = sum(!is.na(value)),
    Missing    = sum(is.na(value)),
    `% missing` = round(100 * mean(is.na(value)), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

No row and no patient is dropped. Missingness is spread across all four measurements (17 missing ages, 14 blood pressures, 20 cholesterol values, 20 BMIs) plus 15 unrecorded genders and 20 unrecorded smoking statuses, so listwise deletion would discard a large share of the file for the sake of complete cases. Instead every summary below uses na.rm = TRUE and reports the number of patients behind each statistic in its own column, so no mean is read without knowing how many observations produced it.

Analysis

Two comparisons, both computed on the long-form data. First, central tendency of each measurement by diagnosis group — mean and median side by side, because the measurements turn out to be pre-binned and a median is the more honest summary of a discretised variable. Second, the difference in mean measurement between self-reported smokers and non-smokers, pooled across diagnosis groups. Counts accompany every figure; nothing is imputed.

Code 
med_summary <- med_tidy |>
  group_by(Measurement = facet_label, Diagnosis = diagnosis_group) |>
  summarise(
    Patients = sum(!is.na(value)),
    Mean     = round(mean(value,   na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Median   = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(Measurement, Diagnosis)

med_summary
Code 
smoker_summary <- med_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(is_smoker), !is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(Measurement = facet_label, is_smoker) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = is_smoker, values_from = c(n, mean_value)) |>
  transmute(
    Measurement,
    `Smokers (n)`      = n_TRUE,
    `Smokers mean`     = round(mean_value_TRUE,  1),
    `Non-smokers (n)`  = n_FALSE,
    `Non-smokers mean` = round(mean_value_FALSE, 1),
    Difference         = round(mean_value_TRUE - mean_value_FALSE, 1)
  )

smoker_summary
Code 
med_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diagnosis_group, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90", outlier.size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ facet_label, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Diagnosis group",
    y = "Measured value",
    caption = "Synthetic teaching dataset; 100 patients, admissions during 2023"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))

Conclusions

The tidy dataset holds 400 patient-measurement rows, of which 329 carry a reported value and 71 are missing. Of 100 patients, 53 are recorded male, 32 female and 15 unrecorded; smoking status splits 40 / 40 with 20 unrecorded.

Differences between diagnosis groups are small. Mean age ranges only from 44.4 to 52 years across groups, and mean blood pressure spans under 6 mmHg. Figure 2 shows why: each measurement takes only five distinct values — age is recorded in ten-year bands, blood pressure in ten-mmHg steps, cholesterol and BMI in five fixed levels each. The variables are pre-binned, which compresses every group difference toward the bin width and makes correlation or regression inappropriate on these columns.

The honest conclusion from this dataset is methodological rather than clinical: with discretised measurements, roughly 18% missingness per measurement, and simulated values, the data supports descriptive comparison of group medians and nothing stronger. The Diagnosis column’s distinction between None (27 patients, examined with no finding) and unrecorded (21 patients) is preserved throughout for the same reason — collapsing them would overstate how many patients are known to be disease-free.

Challenges

  • Rank 7 appears twice (Celine Dion, Pink) and rank 8 is absent, so the ranking will need to be rearranged for

  • The format for the numeric variables will need to be stripped to be solely numbers by removing the dollar signs and commas for more reliable calculations.

Dataset C — Highest-grossing concert tours

Data source

Ranked table of the 20 highest-grossing concert tours by female solo artists, as published on Wikipedia and compiled from Billboard Boxscore figures. Retrieved 2026-10-11, committed unmodified to data/raw/tours_raw.csv, and read here from its GitHub raw URL. The table carries footnote markers and reference numbers from the source page, which are removed during tidying and noted where they changed interpretation.

Code 
high_grossing_women_tours_raw_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shanicesmith98/data-607-assignments/refs/heads/main/week-5-assignment/tours_dataset.csv"

# Everything reads as text: currency columns carry "$" and thousands
# separators, and several numeric cells end in a footnote marker.
tours_raw_data <- read_csv(high_grossing_women_tours_raw_url, col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

Structure before tidying

  <chr> <chr> <chr>           <chr>          <chr>                        <chr> 
1 1     1     2               $780,000,000   $780,000,000                 Taylo…

Twenty rows by 11 columns, one row per tour. Four problems are visible in the head: currency stored as text ("$780,000,000"), footnote markers inside otherwise numeric cells ("2[5]", "$229,100,000[b]"), status symbols inside the tour title ("The Eras Tour †"), and a year range in a single column ("2023–2024") that holds two variables.

Code 
# The two currency column names contain a non-breaking space (U+00A0),
# not a regular space. They look identical on screen, so a rename()
# matching "Actual gross" fails silently.
str_detect(names(tours_raw_data), "\u00a0")
 [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

A fifth problem is not visible at all: Rank is not unique. Rank 7 appears twice and rank 8 is absent, so the column cannot serve as a key.

Transformation steps

Repairing the column names

Code 
# Replace non-breaking spaces with ordinary ones before renaming anything.
names(tours_raw_data) <- names(tours_raw_data) |>
  str_replace_all("\u00a0", " ") |>
  str_trim()

tours <- tours_raw_data |>
  rename(
    source_rank    = Rank,
    peak           = Peak,
    all_time_peak  = `All Time Peak`,
    actual_gross   = `Actual gross`,
    adjusted_gross = `Adjusted gross (in 2022 dollars)`,
    artist         = Artist,
    tour_title     = `Tour title`,
    years          = `Year(s)`,
    shows          = Shows,
    average_gross  = `Average gross`,
    source_ref     = `Ref.`
  )

Capturing the footnote markers before deleting them

Code 
# The dagger marks tours still running when the table was compiled, which
# means their grosses are partial. That is real information, so it is
# captured as a column BEFORE the symbol is stripped out.
tours <- tours |>
  mutate(
    is_ongoing   = str_detect(tour_title, "\u2020"),   # †
    has_marker   = str_detect(tour_title, "[\u2021*]") # ‡ and *
  )

sum(tours$is_ongoing)   # expect 2
[1] 2
Code 
sum(tours$has_marker)   # expect 3
[1] 3

The source page’s legend is not part of the CSV, so the meaning of ‡ and * cannot be recovered from this file. They are recorded in has_marker and flagged as an open question rather than guessed at; the two † tours are treated as incomplete throughout.

Converting text to numbers

Code 
# Helper: remove bracketed footnote references like [4], [a], [21].
strip_notes <- function(x) str_remove_all(x, "\\[[0-9a-z]+\\]")

tours <- tours |>
  mutate(
    # Titles: drop footnotes AND status symbols, then trim the leftover space
    tour_title = tour_title |>
      strip_notes() |>
      str_remove_all("[\u2020\u2021*]") |>
      str_trim(),

    # Peaks: footnotes removed first, then integer conversion
    across(c(peak, all_time_peak), ~ as.integer(strip_notes(.x))),

    # Currency: footnotes first, then parse_number() strips "$" and commas
    across(c(actual_gross, adjusted_gross, average_gross),
           ~ parse_number(strip_notes(.x))),

    across(c(source_rank, shows), as.integer)
  )

Order matters here. parse_number("$229,100,000[b]") applied directly reads the leading number but warns and depends on parser internals; stripping the footnote first makes the conversion unambiguous. For as.integer() the stakes are higher — as.integer("2[5]") returns NA, so six of the seven populated all_time_peak values would silently vanish.

Splitting the year range

Code 
tours <- tours |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    years,
    delim   = "\u2013",                        # EN-DASH, not a hyphen
    names   = c("year_start", "year_end"),
    too_few = "align_start"                    # single-year tours get NA
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(year_start, year_end), as.integer),
    year_end = coalesce(year_end, year_start), # a one-year tour ends the year it starts
    tour_years = year_end - year_start + 1
  )

"2023–2024" is separated by an en-dash (U+2013). Splitting on "-" matches nothing, too_few = "align_start" silently fills every year_end with NA, and all 20 tours appear to be single-year.

Reshaping the two gross figures to long form

Code 
tours_tidy <- tours |>
  # average_gross is derived (actual_gross / shows) and is recomputed below;
  # source_ref is a citation artifact belonging in Sources, not in the data.
  select(-average_gross, -source_ref) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(actual_gross, adjusted_gross),
    names_to  = "gross_basis",
    values_to = "gross_usd"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    gross_basis = if_else(gross_basis == "actual_gross",
                          "Nominal (as earned)",
                          "Adjusted to 2022 USD")
  )

dim(tours_tidy)   # expect 40 x 13
[1] 40 13

Nominal and inflation-adjusted dollars are the same quantity measured on two bases. Side by side in separate columns they invite direct comparison of figures that are not comparable; stacked, the basis becomes an explicit grouping variable and every chart and table must declare which one it uses.

Why the derived column is recomputed

Code 
tours |>
  mutate(
    recomputed = actual_gross / shows,
    difference = round(average_gross - recomputed, 0)
  ) |>
  filter(abs(difference) > 1) |>
  select(tour_title, shows, actual_gross, average_gross, recomputed, difference)
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  tour_title            shows actual_gross average_gross recomputed difference
  <chr>                 <int>        <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 The Monster Ball Tour   203    227400000       1118227   1120197.      -1970

The stored average_gross does not always equal actual_gross / shows. The Monster Ball Tour’s stored average of $1,118,227 across 203 shows implies a gross near $227.0M, while the actual-gross column reads $227.4M. Rather than reconcile the source’s rounding, the per-show figure is recomputed from its components everywhere below.

Analysis

The analysis compares the two gross bases. Each tour is ranked twice — once by nominal gross and once by inflation-adjusted gross — and the difference between those ranks measures how much inflation adjustment changes the standings. Revenue per show is recomputed as actual_gross / shows and reported separately for the 18 completed tours, since the two ongoing tours have partial grosses against a partial show count.

Code 
rank_shift <- tours |>
  mutate(
    rank_nominal  = rank(-actual_gross,   ties.method = "min"),
    rank_adjusted = rank(-adjusted_gross, ties.method = "min"),
    rank_change   = rank_nominal - rank_adjusted   # positive = climbs
  ) |>
  arrange(rank_adjusted)
Code 
rank_shift |>
  filter(abs(rank_change) >= 2) |>
  transmute(
    Artist                  = artist,
    Tour                    = tour_title,
    Years                   = str_c(year_start, "-", year_end),
    `Nominal rank`          = rank_nominal,
    `Adjusted rank`         = rank_adjusted,
    `Places moved`          = rank_change
  )
Code 
tours |>
  filter(!is_ongoing) |>
  mutate(gross_per_show = actual_gross / shows) |>
  slice_max(gross_per_show, n = 8) |>
  transmute(
    Artist              = artist,
    Tour                = tour_title,
    Shows               = shows,
    `Actual gross ($M)` = round(actual_gross / 1e6, 1),
    `Per show ($M)`     = round(gross_per_show / 1e6, 2)
  )
Code 
# Order the y-axis by adjusted gross so the chart reads as a ranking
title_order <- tours |> arrange(adjusted_gross) |> pull(tour_title)

tours_tidy |>
  mutate(tour_title = factor(tour_title, levels = title_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gross_usd / 1e6, y = tour_title)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = tour_title), color = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = gross_basis), size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("$", x, "M")) +
  labs(
    x       = "Tour gross",
    y       = NULL,
    color   = "Basis",
    caption = "Source: Wikipedia ranking of highest-grossing female solo tours, compiled from Billboard Boxscore"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

Conclusions

The tidy dataset holds 40 rows — 20 tours on two gross bases. Nominal grosses total $5.76 billion against $6.88 billion adjusted to 2022 dollars, a difference of 19% concentrated entirely in the older tours.

Inflation adjustment reorders the table. Figure 3 shows the two bases diverging as tours get older: recent tours sit as single near-overlapping points, while mid-2000s tours show a wide gap. Cher’s Living Proof: The Farewell Tour climbs from 14th on nominal gross to 10th adjusted, while Pink’s Summer Carnival falls from 8th to 14th — not because it earned less, but because it has no inflation to accumulate and older tours pass it.

Revenue per show separates two business models that total gross conceals. Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour earned about $13.9M per show across 56 shows, roughly 23 times Cher’s $0.6M per show — yet Cher’s 325-show farewell run still placed 10th on adjusted gross. High-grossing tours reach the top either through stadium economics on a short run or through volume over several years.

Three limitations follow from the raw structure. source_rank is not unique — rank 7 is shared and rank 8 absent — so it is kept only as provenance and never used as a key. all_time_peak is missing for 14 of 20 tours and is excluded from analysis. And 2 tours were still running at compilation, so their figures are partial and they are removed from the per-show comparison.
